passage: Shalini, you think your father was always this calm about cricket? Your grandmother remembers. When Zorama was ten, here in Aizawl, he had one hero, an opening batsman. The wall above his bed held newspaper cuttings of that man's centuries, only centuries. When the batsman scored three runs in a big match, Zorama said the umpire had cheated. Out for nothing the next week? The wet pitch. I asked him, "Beta, how many times has he failed this year?" He counted two. I found the sports page and we counted together. It was seven. He went red and stomped off. That evening I saw him pin up a small report of a bad score too, in the corner. I, Lalremsiami, was never prouder of a scrap of newspaper.

qa.q: Where were the newspaper cuttings of the batsman's centuries?
qa.a: On the wall above Zorama's bed.

qa.q: Why did it feel reasonable to young Zorama that the umpire had cheated?
qa.a: He loved his hero so much that a bad score felt like it could not be the batsman's fault. Blaming the umpire or the pitch kept his picture of the best player safe.

qa.q: What choice did Lalremsiami make that helped Zorama see more of the record?
qa.a: Instead of arguing, Lalremsiami asked him to count the failures and then counted them with him from the sports page. The real number, seven, was hard to ignore.

qa.q: How might Shalini see Zorama after hearing this story?
qa.a: Shalini may find it funny and warm that a calm father was once a stubborn fan, and it may help Shalini notice when only the good bits about a favourite get remembered. 😊

grounding: A grandmother recalls a boy, now Shalini's father, who remembered only his hero's centuries and blamed bad scores on the umpire or the pitch.

passage: The Nagpur wedding hall was deafening, and the only way to follow the match was Vidya's phone, which kept losing signal. Her cousin Raghav, nine, pressed against her elbow. "He'll hit a fifty. He always does." The score froze, then jumped: his favourite all-rounder, out for four. Raghav didn't blink. "That ball was unplayable. Plus the umpire is from the other side." "The replay showed it was a normal ball," Vidya said, shouting over the band. "No, remember last month? Eighty-two against the same team." "And the two ducks before that?" Raghav frowned as if she'd spoken another language. "Those were bad luck." The dhol started again. Vidya gave up, but noticed he never mentioned the ducks when he told his uncles the story at dinner.

qa.q: How many runs did Raghav's favourite all-rounder score before getting out?
qa.a: He was out for four.

qa.q: Why does Raghav blame the ball and the umpire instead of his hero?
qa.a: To him the all-rounder is simply the best, so a low score must have an outside cause. Holding on to the eighty-two feels like proof, while the ducks feel like accidents.

qa.q: Vidya gave up arguing over the band. What could she try at a quieter moment instead?
qa.a: She could make a game of writing down every score for the next few matches, good and bad, and look at the list with Raghav. Seeing all the numbers together is harder to explain away than one argument.

qa.q: What might the uncles at dinner believe after hearing Raghav's version?
qa.a: They would only hear about the eighty-two and the unplayable ball, so they might think the all-rounder is doing better than he really is.

grounding: A boy at a noisy wedding explains his favourite player's low score as a bad ball and a biased umpire, and leaves out the recent ducks.

passage: Okay, so you want to know about Joseph? Didi, I'm telling you, that guy is fake. I'm Anjali, I've sat two rows behind him since June, and I've got receipts. Monday he sends "all the best everyone!!" to the class group before the test. Who does that? Attention. Wednesday he posts a photo helping Ma'am carry books. Obviously for likes. What? No, I didn't see what he wrote to Farah when her grandmother was sick. I just scroll past his long messages, they're boring. And my feed keeps showing me those videos about fake-nice people, so it's not just me, it's a whole thing. Swati agrees with me too. Mostly. Why are you looking at me like that? Fine, show me the message to Farah then. ...Okay, that one's nice. But one message doesn't mean anything.

qa.q: What did Joseph send to the class group on Monday?
qa.a: He sent "all the best everyone!!" before the test.

qa.q: Why does Anjali feel so sure that Joseph is fake?
qa.a: Every message Anjali chooses to read seems to fit, and the feed and a friend seem to agree, so it feels like a pile of proof. Anjali doesn't notice the skipped long, kind messages.

qa.q: When Anjali finally reads the message to Farah, what choice could Anjali make to test that view?
qa.a: Anjali could go back and read all of Joseph's messages, not only the ones that look like showing off, and ask what a kind person would have written.

qa.q: If you were Joseph, how might you feel if you learned Anjali had decided you were fake?
qa.a: Hurt and confused, because everything friendly Joseph does is being read as a trick, so there is no way to change Anjali's mind by being nice.

grounding: A teenager talks to an older sister about a classmate judged to be fake, reads his messages only for proof, and skips his kind ones.

passage: I'm Jyoti, and I sit next to Ankita in Class 10. I'm writing down what I saw, because I'm not sure what's going on in her head. Since the new girl, Ritwika, laughed during Ankita's presentation, Ankita checks Ritwika's every post. At lunch she'll hold out her phone: "See, she put an eye-roll on my joke." When Ritwika sent a birthday wish to Ankita in the group, Ankita didn't mention it at all. I only saw it later, scrolling up. Last week Ritwika offered to share her notes before the chemistry test. Ankita said, "She wants us to owe her." And the reels Ankita shows me are all about two-faced classmates now. Maybe she's right about Ritwika. I honestly can't tell. But she only ever shows me one kind of message.

qa.q: Who sent Ankita a birthday wish in the group?
qa.a: Ritwika sent a birthday wish to Ankita in the group.

qa.q: Why might Ankita believe Ritwika only offered notes because "she wants us to owe her"?
qa.a: Ankita has already decided Ritwika is fake after the laugh during the presentation, so even kind acts get read as tricks. That reading feels sensible to her because it matches everything else she has picked out.

qa.q: What could Jyoti say to Ankita that might open a crack in her view?
qa.a: Jyoti could scroll up and show the birthday wish, asking gently how that fits. Asking a question is easier to hear than being told she is wrong.

qa.q: How might Ritwika feel about Ankita's coldness?
qa.a: Ritwika may feel confused and shut out, since her birthday wish and offer of notes got nothing back. She may not even know the laugh caused it.

grounding: A classmate describes how a teenager has decided another girl is fake, reads posts only for proof and ignores the friendly ones.

passage: The career cell at the college in Guwahati had a sign-up sheet for placements, and Sabina walked past it for the third time. She had made up her mind a month ago: skip placements, study full-time for the MBA entrance. In the library she opened her laptop and searched "why placements are a trap." She saved four articles. Then she messaged two seniors who had dropped placements and cleared the exam. Both wrote back, "Best decision of my life." That evening she told her friend Bhupen, "I've done so much research. Everyone agrees." "Did you ask Dimpy-di? She didn't clear it and had no job for a year." Sabina shrugged. "Her case was different." "And the placement officer?" "They just want numbers." She closed the laptop, feeling thoroughly prepared.

qa.q: How many articles did Sabina save?
qa.a: She saved four articles.

qa.q: Why does Sabina feel "thoroughly prepared"?
qa.a: She has read articles and heard from seniors, so it feels like a lot of research. But every source she chose already agreed with her, so it feels complete without being balanced.

qa.q: What choice could Sabina make before the placement deadline to test her decision?
qa.a: She could talk to Dimpy-di and the placement officer, the people most likely to disagree, and ask what went wrong for those who didn't clear the exam.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel when Sabina dismisses each question?
qa.a: Bhupen may feel unheard and a little worried, since the questions were meant to help, and may decide to stop raising doubts.

grounding: A college student searches only for articles and seniors that support skipping placements and dismisses those who might disagree.

passage: Alejandro had decided to skip the graduate recruitment fair at his university in Cape Town. He was going to build his cycling channel on a video site full-time. On Sunday he spent six hours "researching." He watched interviews with three creators who had quit their jobs and hit big numbers. He read a blog called "Your degree is a safety net you don't need." He even bookmarked a comment from a stranger: "Just go for it, bro." When his flatmate Zanele sent him an article about how few channels earn enough to pay rent, he replied with a thumbs-up and didn't open it. "I've looked at this from every angle," he told her over supper. Zanele pushed her plate aside. "Every angle that agrees with you, maybe." Alejandro laughed and went back to his notes.

qa.q: How long did Alejandro spend "researching" on Sunday?
qa.a: He spent six hours.

qa.q: Why did Alejandro reply with a thumbs-up but not open Zanele's article?
qa.a: He had already made his choice, and an article about low earnings threatened it. Staying with the encouraging stories let him keep feeling well informed and sure.

qa.q: Zanele's comment at supper was a turning point Alejandro laughed off. What could he do with it instead?
qa.a: He could list the three strongest reasons against his plan and read Zanele's article before the fair closes, then decide whether a job plus the channel on weekends might work.

qa.q: What might be going through Zanele's mind when she pushes her plate aside?
qa.a: She is probably frustrated and worried, because she can see Alejandro only collecting cheers and feels her article was ignored.

grounding: A student abroad collects only creators' success stories to support skipping the recruitment fair and ignores his flatmate's article.

passage: Asif, beta, before you tell your friend his idea is rubbish, listen to your phuphi. In 1994, at nineteen, I shared a hostel room in Pune with Pushpa. She wanted to open a cassette-lending library for the girls' hostels. Every time someone said, "Everyone copies cassettes for free," Pushpa said, "They're just jealous." But when one girl said, "What a cute idea," Pushpa repeated it for days. I tried arguing. Price, rent, damaged tapes. Each point she swatted away, and she got more stubborn. So one night I, Irawati, said something different. "Pushpa, I've noticed you remember every nice comment and forget every worry. I only say it because I want this to work." She was quiet for a long time. Then she asked me to list the worries. She never opened the library. She ran a very good photocopy stall instead.

qa.q: What did Pushpa want to open?
qa.a: A cassette-lending library for the girls' hostels.

qa.q: Why did Pushpa keep repeating "What a cute idea" for days?
qa.a: The praise made her feel her plan was right, while warnings felt like attacks. Holding on to the kind words protected her hope.

qa.q: What made Irawati's second approach work better than arguing?
qa.a: She stopped fighting point by point and gently named the pattern she saw, saying it came from wanting the idea to work. That let Pushpa listen instead of defend.

qa.q: How might Pushpa have felt when Irawati named the pattern?
qa.a: She probably felt stung at first, since she went quiet for a long time, but also cared for, because she then asked for the list of worries.

grounding: An aunt recalls watching a college roommate dismiss warnings about a business idea, and how kindly naming the pattern worked where arguing had not.

passage: The deposit for the café space was due at ten the next morning, and the power had gone out across the whole block in Indiranagar. By candlelight, Vinita watched her flatmate Tejas scroll through comments on his board-game café plan. "Look, forty people said they'd come!" he said. "Tejas, the landlord said the rent goes up in six months." "He's bluffing." "And Arun said weekday evenings are dead there." "Arun hates fun." Vinita felt the urge to list every problem again. She'd done that twice; he'd only dug in. Instead she said, "Can I tell you something I've noticed? Every doubt gets a reason it doesn't count, and every nice comment gets read out loud. I'm on your side. That's why I'm saying it." Tejas stopped scrolling. The candle flickered. "Okay," he said at last. "Say the doubts again. Slowly."

qa.q: When was the deposit for the café space due?
qa.a: At ten the next morning.

qa.q: Why does Tejas say "He's bluffing" and "Arun hates fun"?
qa.a: Tejas wants the café so badly that each doubt feels like a threat to the dream, so he finds a quick reason to wave it away. The forty positive comments feel like real proof.

qa.q: With the deadline so close, what did Vinita choose to do differently, and why did it work?
qa.a: She stopped listing problems and instead kindly described the pattern she saw, saying she was on his side. That made Tejas curious rather than defensive.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel sitting in the dark before she spoke?
qa.a: She may feel torn and anxious, wanting to support Tejas but worried he will lose his deposit on a shaky plan. 😟

grounding: A flatmate sees a friend wave off every warning about a café plan while reading out encouragement, and kindly names the pattern the night before the deposit is due.

passage:
Week one. At the Jaipur hotel's front desk, Jagdish, the shift supervisor, watched the new trainee, Afreen, freeze for a moment when a guest asked about the airport shuttle. He made a note in his head: slow. When she printed the wrong invoice that afternoon, he thought, there it is.
Week three. A family from Lyon praised Afreen by name in the feedback book for sorting out their lost luggage. Jagdish skimmed it and turned the page. That same evening she mistyped a room number, and he told the manager, "I did say she might not be right for the desk."
Week five. Preparing her review, Jagdish pulled up the logs to prove his point. Her check-ins were the fastest on the shift. He stared at the screen for a long moment, then deleted the first line he had written.

qa.q: What did the family from Lyon praise Afreen for?
qa.a: For sorting out their lost luggage.

qa.q: Why did Jagdish think "there it is" when Afreen printed the wrong invoice?
qa.a: He had already decided she was slow on day one, so the slip felt like proof. Each new mistake seemed to confirm what he believed.

qa.q: In week five, what did Jagdish do that changed the review?
qa.a: He looked at the actual check-in logs, which showed Afreen was the fastest on the shift, and deleted the unfair first line. Checking the record instead of his memory was the turning point.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt working under Jagdish in the first weeks?
qa.a: She may have sensed his doubt and felt nervous or watched, even while doing good work that seemed to go unnoticed.

grounding: A supervisor who judged a new trainee as weak on day one reads her slips as proof and skims her praise, until the logs show otherwise.

passage: Santosh, you're new to reviewing people, so let me confess something. In 1999 I was a young man of twenty-five, a sub-editor at a Lucknow newspaper, and they put a new reporter, Kamini, on my desk. On her first day she spelt a minister's title wrong. That was it for me. I'm Lalit, and I decided she was careless. After that, every comma she missed went into my little notebook. Her scoop on the flooded school? I told myself someone had tipped her off. Her clean copy on budget day? Luck. At the six-month review I read out my notebook. The editor listened, then pulled out a folder of her bylines and asked, "And these?" I had no answer. I'd been collecting only one kind of fact. So before you write anyone's review, look for what you've been skipping.

qa.q: What mistake did Kamini make on her first day?
qa.a: She spelt a minister's title wrong.

qa.q: Why did young Lalit put every missed comma into his notebook?
qa.a: Having decided early that Kamini was careless, he looked for proof and felt he was simply being thorough. Good work didn't fit, so he explained it away as luck or a tip-off.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Lalit at the six-month review?
qa.a: The editor pulled out Kamini's bylines and asked "And these?", showing him the evidence he had been skipping.

qa.q: How might Kamini have felt if she had known about the notebook?
qa.a: She would likely have felt judged unfairly and discouraged, since her scoop and clean copy were being dismissed.

grounding: An older editor tells a new reviewer how he once judged a new reporter careless and noted only her slips, ignoring her good work.

passage:
"Asif, I need you to argue against me tonight. Properly."
"Against the no-homework plan?" He put down his roti. "Gladly. I think it's a mistake."
"Good. That's why I asked you and not Mummy." Irawati opened her notebook. "First, what would make me drop the idea?"
"If Class 3 marks fall in the spring test."
"Written down. What else?"
"Parents who can't help at home might want practice sheets. You'd take away the one structure some kids have."
Irawati paused. "That's a good point. I hadn't thought of it."
Mummy smiled. "You two usually shout."
"Not tonight. He's my best critic." She turned back. "What's your strongest argument?"
Asif thought. "Kids forget without repetition."
"Then I'll ask the principal for a trial with an optional practice corner, and check marks after one term."
"Hmm. That's… actually fair."

qa.q: What would make Irawati drop the idea, according to Asif?
qa.a: If Class 3 marks fall in the spring test.

qa.q: Why does Irawati say "That's a good point" instead of defending herself?
qa.a: She wants to find the weak spots before committing, so a strong objection feels useful rather than insulting. She sees disagreement as information.

qa.q: Which choice did Irawati make after hearing Asif's strongest argument?
qa.a: She changed the plan to a trial with an optional practice corner and a check on marks after one term, building his concern into her proposal.

qa.q: How might Asif feel about being called "my best critic"?
qa.a: He probably feels respected and taken seriously, which is why he ends up calling her plan "actually fair" instead of just arguing.

grounding: A young teacher asks her brother to argue the case against her plan, sets what would change her mind, and adjusts the plan.

passage: I'm Vinita, and last spring I was certain. As the newest product designer at our Kochi office, I wanted to remove the password login and let people sign in with a one-time code only. Cleaner, faster. I'd already made the slides. But I'd been burned before by being sure. So I wrote on a sticky note: "What would change my mind?" My answer: if older users got stuck more. Then I did the uncomfortable part. I asked Rafiq, the engineer who questions everything, to give me the best case against it. He took it seriously. He showed me support tickets from people with bad signal who never got the code. I read them all, even though my ears were burning. We ended up keeping both options. My slides were worse. The product was better. Rafiq still calls me "Madam Certain" and brings me tea when he disagrees.

qa.q: What did Vinita write on the sticky note?
qa.a: She wrote, "What would change my mind?"

qa.q: How did Vinita feel reading the support tickets, and why did she keep reading?
qa.a: Her ears were burning, so she felt embarrassed or defensive, but she kept going because she wanted to know if she was wrong before committing.

qa.q: Which choice made the biggest difference to the final product?
qa.a: Asking Rafiq, the person most likely to disagree, for the best case against the idea. His tickets showed a real problem she hadn't seen.

qa.q: How might Rafiq see Vinita after she asked him to argue against her?
qa.a: He likely respects her more and feels his doubts are welcome, which is why he now brings her tea when he disagrees. 🙂

grounding: A young designer asks what would change her mind, seeks out a sharp critic and reads the best case against her plan before committing.

passage: Abhinav, you think you're a good bargainer? Let me tell you about your Dada at nine, in Bhopal, 1968. At the Muharram fair a boy had a tin box of glittery animal stickers. I asked the price. "Two rupees for the tiger," he said. Two rupees! My whole pocket money for a month was three. I said, "One rupee." He said, "One-fifty, final." I felt I'd beaten him. I, Yusuf, walked off holding that tiger like a trophy. At the next stall a man was selling the same tigers. Four annas each. Four annas! I stood there with my mouth open. That boy had simply picked a big number first, and I had bargained down from his number, not from what the tiger was worth.

qa.q: How much did the boy first ask for the tiger sticker?
qa.a: Two rupees for the tiger.

qa.q: Why did young Yusuf feel he had beaten the boy?
qa.a: He measured the deal against the two rupees he first heard, so one rupee fifty felt like a big saving. He didn't know the real price, so the first number felt like the fair one.

qa.q: What could Yusuf have done at the fair before paying?
qa.a: He could have walked around the other stalls first to see what the same stickers cost, so he had his own idea of a fair price.

qa.q: How might the boy with the tin box have felt as Yusuf walked away?
qa.a: He was probably pleased, since his big opening price had worked and he got far more than the stickers sold for next door.

grounding: A grandfather recalls bargaining for a sticker as a boy, treating the seller's first high price as the baseline and feeling he'd won.

passage: The church-yard jumble sale in Kochi was closing in ten minutes, and rain had started on the tarpaulins. Noor, nine, clutched sixty rupees and stopped at the table where a teenager called Thomas was selling a sticker album of space rockets. "How much?" "Three hundred." Noor's stomach dropped. Three hundred was impossible. "Can I have it for… a hundred and fifty?" "Two hundred." "A hundred?" The rain got louder. Thomas started folding his tablecloth. "Fine. Last price, eighty." Noor felt she was winning big. Eighty was so much less than three hundred! She borrowed twenty from her cousin and paid, grinning. On the way home, her cousin said quietly, "That album is thirty in the bookshop near school." Noor looked at the wet album and said nothing for a while.

qa.q: How much did Thomas first ask for the sticker album?
qa.a: Three hundred.

qa.q: Why did eighty rupees feel like a big win to Noor?
qa.a: She compared it with the three hundred she heard first, so eighty seemed tiny. The rain and closing time also rushed her, leaving no chance to think about the real price.

qa.q: With the sale closing and rain starting, what could Noor have tried instead?
qa.a: She could have asked her cousin what such albums usually cost, or decided her own top price before hearing any number, and walked away if it was higher.

qa.q: How might Noor's cousin have felt lending her twenty rupees?
qa.a: The cousin may have felt uneasy watching the deal and waited until afterwards to say something gently, not wanting to spoil the moment in the rain.

grounding: A girl at a closing jumble sale bargains down from a high first price and feels she has won, though the final price is still too high.

passage:
Dear Rekha Aunty,
Thank you for helping me with physics before the term tests. I wanted to tell you how they went, and honestly, I'm upset. I got 70. In the first unit test in July I got 90, and you wrote "Brilliant, Kunal!" on my paper. So 70 feels like I've gone downhill completely. I didn't eat much at dinner.
The strange part is my friend Charu also got 70. Her first test was 50, and she was dancing in the corridor. Same mark. She's thrilled, I'm miserable. Maa says 70 is still above the class average and I'm being a silly boy.
I keep looking at that 90 and thinking that's who I really am.
Can we do motion and force again on Saturday?
Your student,
Kunal

qa.q: What mark did Charu get in her first test?
qa.a: Her first test was 50.

qa.q: Why does 70 feel like "downhill" to Kunal when it makes Charu happy?
qa.a: Kunal is measuring against his first mark of 90, so 70 feels like a loss. Charu is measuring against her 50, so the same number feels like a jump.

qa.q: What could Kunal do to judge the 70 more fairly?
qa.a: He could look at what he actually got wrong this time and compare his mark with the class average Maa mentioned, instead of only with the 90.

qa.q: If you were Rekha Aunty reading this, how might you feel?
qa.a: You might feel sad that Kunal is so hard on himself but glad he wrote and asked for Saturday help, and you might want to show him that 70 is still solid work.

grounding: A teenage boy writes that scoring 70 after a first test of 90 feels terrible, while his friend is thrilled with 70 after 50.

passage: Simran didi, don't laugh, okay? I know it's just a Hindi test. I got 70. You know what I got in the first one? 90. Ninety! Papa put it on the fridge and called me his clever boy. So now I'm sitting here thinking I've ruined everything. And Rekha, from my tuition, she got 70 too, same as me. Her first one was 50. She sent a voice note screaming, "Seventy, yaar!" She's happy and I'm on the terrace sulking. Same number. Isn't that weird? If I'd got 50 first, I'd be celebrating right now, wouldn't I? ... Maybe I would. Fine. I'm Farhan, and I'm still annoyed. But maybe 70 isn't a disaster. Can you help me see which questions I lost marks on? Not tonight. Tomorrow.

qa.q: Where is Farhan sitting while he talks to Simran didi?
qa.a: On the terrace, sulking.

qa.q: Why does Farhan feel he has ruined everything with a 70?
qa.a: His first result was 90 and it went on the fridge, so that number has become his standard. Anything below it feels like failure.

qa.q: What choice does Farhan make at the end of the conversation, and why is it useful?
qa.a: He asks Simran didi to help him see which questions he lost marks on, tomorrow. That moves him from comparing numbers to learning from the paper.

qa.q: How might Simran didi feel listening to her brother's worry?
qa.a: She might want to smile at how dramatic he is but also feel for him, since she can see the same 70 means very different things to him and to Rekha.

grounding: A teenage boy tells his sister how 70 after a first score of 90 feels terrible, while a friend is thrilled with 70 after 50.

passage:
"Mummy, the café in Bandra replied! They want a menu design."
"Wah, Rajni! How much are they paying?"
"They said… three thousand for the whole menu."
Her brother Vishal looked up from his phone. "Three thousand? What did you plan to ask?"
"I'd read that freelancers charge eight to ten for a menu. But now ten sounds greedy after three."
"So what are you going to say?"
"Maybe four? Four-five hundred?"
"Didi, your own research said eight."
"I know, but they said three first. If I say eight, they'll think I'm crazy."
Mummy put the tea down. "Beta, why is their number more real than yours?"
Rajni opened her mouth, then shut it. "I don't know."
"Try seven-five," said Vishal. "Explain why."
She typed "4,500," deleted it, and sat staring at the empty reply box.

qa.q: How much did the café first offer Rajni for the whole menu?
qa.a: Three thousand for the whole menu.

qa.q: Why does ten thousand suddenly sound greedy to Rajni?
qa.a: After hearing three thousand first, that number has become her reference point, so her own research figure now feels too big, even though she believes the research.

qa.q: Mummy's question, "why is their number more real than yours?", is a turning point. What could Rajni do with it?
qa.a: She could reply with a figure based on her research, such as seven-five, and explain what the work involves, instead of starting from the café's number.

qa.q: How might Vishal feel watching his sister shrink her price?
qa.a: He is probably frustrated and protective, since he can see she is underselling her work, which is why he pushes her to try seven-five.

grounding: A young designer anchors on a café's low first offer and adjusts too little from it, while her brother and mother question the anchor.

passage: I'm Tejas, and this is the story of how I paid too much for a motorbike and felt clever about it. It was my final year in Nashik. I'd checked the listings: that model, that year, around forty thousand. Then I went to see Hrithik's bike. He's a friendly guy, and before I could say anything, he said, "Sixty-five. Look at the tyres." Sixty-five! My forty suddenly felt silly, like I hadn't done the research. I said fifty. He said sixty. We went back and forth while his mother brought us chai. We settled at fifty-four, and I rode home feeling like the smartest man in Nashik: I'd knocked off eleven thousand. It was a week before I looked at the listings again. Fourteen thousand more than I'd planned. His first number did the bargaining for him.

qa.q: What price did Tejas find in the listings for that model?
qa.a: Around forty thousand.

qa.q: Why did Tejas's forty suddenly feel silly?
qa.a: Once Hrithik said sixty-five, that number became the reference point, and Tejas started doubting his own research instead of the seller's figure.

qa.q: At what moment could Tejas have changed the outcome, and how?
qa.a: Right after hearing sixty-five, he could have said his research showed about forty and started from there, instead of bargaining down from Hrithik's number.

qa.q: How might Hrithik remember the sale?
qa.a: Hrithik probably thinks it was a fair, friendly deal over chai and may not even see the opening price as a trick.

grounding: A final-year student bargains down from a seller's high first price and pays well above his own researched figure, feeling he won.

passage: The school's bus contract came up every March, and Moinak, the youngest teacher on the committee, had watched it happen twice. Each year the contractor walked into the staff room, said a number before anyone sat down, and the whole meeting circled around it. Last year he'd opened at ninety thousand a month, and Principal Alka had felt good about getting him to eighty. This year Moinak got ready. He called three other bus operators, looked up the fuel costs, and worked out a range: sixty-five to seventy-two. He showed Alka and the accountant, Jasleen, on Monday. "If he says ninety again, we don't bargain from ninety," he said. "We start from our numbers." On Friday the contractor said, "Ninety-five." Alka glanced at Moinak's sheet and said calmly, "Our research says sixty-eight. Let's talk from there."

qa.q: What range did Moinak work out?
qa.a: Sixty-five to seventy-two.

qa.q: Why did Principal Alka feel good about eighty last year?
qa.a: Alka was comparing it with the contractor's opening ninety thousand, so eighty felt like a win, even though there was no research to show what was fair.

qa.q: Which choice by the committee changed the negotiation this year?
qa.a: Preparing a range from other operators' quotes and fuel costs beforehand, then answering the opening number with their own figure instead of bargaining down from it.

qa.q: How might the contractor feel when Alka replies with sixty-eight?
qa.a: He may be surprised and unsettled, since his high first figure no longer sets the terms, and he has to argue from their research instead.

grounding: A young teacher notices that the contractor's first figure shapes the bus contract talks, and prepares his own researched range.

Subject: Before Thursday's venue call
Hi Dhruv,
Quick thought before we speak to the banquet hall. You know me, I'm my father's son and I check every price. I've sat in on four venue negotiations since I joined, and I've noticed something. Whoever says a number first seems to own the rest of the meeting. In June the manager opened at 2.5 lakh, we "won" it down to 2.1, and everyone celebrated. But the two halls nearby charge about 1.6 for the same size.
So this time I've done homework. Three comparable halls, their off-season rates, and our guest numbers. My range is 1.5 to 1.75. If they open high, I'd like us to calmly say our figure and our reasons, not start bargaining from theirs.
I've attached the sheet. Tell me if you think I'm missing anything.
Thanks,
Yogesh

qa.a: About 1.6.

qa.q: What worries Yogesh about how the June negotiation went?

qa.q: What choice does Yogesh suggest for Thursday's call, and why?

qa.q: How might Dhruv react to this email?

grounding: A young man emails a colleague after noticing that the first number sets the talks, and proposes a range built from research.
